standard.title: Analyse Data for Patterns and Anomalies
standard.description: analyse and connect a variety of data and information to identify and explain patterns, trends, relationships and anomalies
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify patterns and anomalies in data and explain observations using scientific knowledge (AC9S7I05). They have not yet connected data across multiple sources to support an explanation, or used proportional reasoning and extrapolation as analytical tools at this level.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse data from their own investigations and secondary sources to identify and explain patterns, trends, proportional relationships and anomalies — connecting multiple data sources where relevant and using scientific knowledge to account for observed patterns. Students can discuss the validity of extrapolations from their data and highlight inconsistencies across data sources.

nodes.label: Identifying patterns, trends and relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify patterns (repeating features), trends (directional change over a variable) and relationships (one variable changing in response to another) in data sets, using appropriate descriptive language.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one pattern or trend in a described data set and describe it in specific terms — stating the direction, the variables involved, and the nature of the change (e.g. 'as X increases, Y increases proportionally').
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe patterns, trends and relationships across two or three different data representations — using precise language to describe the nature of the relationship (proportional, inverse, non-linear) and the conditions under which it holds.
wider: Analyse data from atmospheric monitoring and ice cores to identify patterns and trends in atmospheric CO₂ — examining long-term trend vs. seasonal variation as different pattern types in the same data set.

Analyse data on heat transfer through insulating material layers to identify a proportional relationship (e.g. doubled thickness → halved heat transfer) — connecting pattern analysis to quantitative reasoning.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who describe patterns in vague terms ('it goes up') rather than precise relational language cannot explain them scientifically or identify anomalies against them (Node 2). The precision of pattern description determines whether the subsequent analysis is substantive.

response_modes.reason: Precise pattern description is a language skill requiring practice. Students consistently drop the variable names, direction, and nature of the relationship — reverting to 'the line goes up'. Practice with feedback on language precision — specifically requiring the student to name both variables and the direction of change — builds the habit.

success_criteria: Can describe a pattern or trend naming both variables and the direction of change.
Can distinguish between a trend (directional change), a pattern (repeating feature) and a relationship (covariance).
Does not use vague language like 'it goes up' — uses the variable names.

nodes.label: Identifying and explaining anomalies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify anomalies in data — data points that do not fit the identified pattern — and propose explanations for them in terms of measurement error, procedural variation or genuine outliers.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify an anomalous data point in a provided data set and give one plausible explanation for why it differs from the pattern (measurement error, equipment malfunction, genuine variation).
nodes.typical_width: Identify anomalies and evaluate at least two possible explanations — distinguishing between errors that should be excluded and genuine outliers that may warrant further investigation — using evidence to support the preferred explanation.
wider: Compare published data with experimental data for the same measurement (e.g. sound insulation levels) and identify patterns in the differences — examining whether differences are systematic (suggesting a procedural issue) or random.

Examine tables, graphs and simulations of radioactive decay to predict changes in mass over time — using the pattern to identify which data points are anomalous and evaluating whether they reflect real decay variation or simulation error.
success_criteria: Can identify an anomalous data point as one that does not fit the identified pattern.
Can propose a plausible explanation for an anomaly that distinguishes between error and genuine variation.
Does not treat all anomalies the same — can evaluate whether an anomaly should be excluded or investigated.

nodes.label: Connecting and comparing data sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can connect and compare data from multiple sources to identify consistencies, inconsistencies and what they mean for scientific claims — including discussing the validity of extrapolation from data.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare data from two sources on the same topic, identify one point of consistency and one inconsistency, and explain what the inconsistency means for the confidence of the conclusion.
nodes.typical_width: Connect data from multiple sources — primary data from an investigation and secondary published data — to evaluate whether findings are consistent, identifying inconsistencies and discussing their implications for the validity of conclusions. Discuss the validity of extrapolating beyond the data collected.
wider: Analyse representations of data from atmospheric monitoring and ice cores to highlight inconsistencies — examining how scientists deal with data from different sources that don't perfectly align.

Examine the validity of extrapolating from experimental data (e.g. extrapolating a heating curve beyond the measured range) — considering what assumptions are required and when extrapolation is or isn't justified.

response_modes.reason: Multi-source data connection requires integrating pattern identification (Node 1), anomaly analysis (Node 2) and validity reasoning (AC9S9I06) into a coherent analytical judgment: 'These sources agree on X; they disagree on Y; the disagreement suggests Z about the reliability of one or both.' This integration is the descriptor's analytical demand.

success_criteria: Can identify consistency and inconsistency across two data sources on the same topic.
Can explain what an inconsistency implies for confidence in a conclusion.
Can discuss the validity of an extrapolation — identifying the assumption it requires.
